hero.heading: Maintenance & Off-Season Guide
hero.subheading: Based on what experienced builders recommend: a home gasifier runs part-time, not continuously. That means scheduled maintenance, proper shutdown procedures, and a startup checklist that catches problems before they become failures.

body.text: Unlike a car you drive daily, a home gasifier might sit idle for weeks between runs. According to builders who have run these systems, that idle time is when corrosion sets in, tar hardens in filters, and small leaks go unnoticed. A simple maintenance routine — 15 minutes after each run, a monthly inspection, and a proper seasonal shutdown — is what keeps a system reliable.

The schedules below are based on typical home-scale operation as described in the literature: 4–8 hours per run, 1–3 runs per week during active season. Adjust intervals based on your actual run time and fuel quality.

tasks.task: Allow the reactor to cool with the air inlet open — never seal a hot reactor
Check the condensate drain and empty if more than half full
Note any unusual smells, sounds, or performance changes while memory is fresh
Check the gas outlet for tar drips — wipe clean before they harden
Log run time, fuel used, and any observations in your maintenance log
Inspect and clean the filter — check pressure drop, replace media if clogged
Check all gas line connections for leaks using soapy water
Inspect the reactor grate — shake or poke to confirm ash isn't bridging
Verify CO detector is functional — press test button
Check fuel supply — confirm moisture under 20% with a meter
Inspect the hopper lid seal — replace if cracked or brittle

schedules.title: Monthly inspection
schedules.timing: Once per month during active season

tasks.task: Inspect all welds for cracks, especially around the tuyere and grate area
Check refractory lining for cracks or spalling — patch with refractory cement
Inspect the ash removal port seal and gasket
Clean the condensate collection system thoroughly — flush with water
Replace CO detector batteries if not on a sealed unit
Check all bolted connections — thermal cycling loosens fasteners over time
Inspect the gas cooling section for tar accumulation
Run the reactor until the fuel bed is fully consumed — don't store with char in the reactor
Allow to cool completely — at least 24 hours — before any storage prep
Remove all ash and char from the reactor, grate, and ash pit
Flush the condensate system and dispose of tar condensate as hazardous waste
Remove and clean all filter media — store dry in a sealed container
Cover all inlets and outlets with weatherproof caps to prevent moisture and pest ingress
Apply a light coat of high-temp anti-rust spray to exposed metal surfaces
Store the unit under cover — a tarp is minimum; a shed is better
Document any issues to address before spring startup

schedules.title: Spring startup
schedules.timing: Before first run of the season

tasks.task: Inspect all welds and the reactor body for winter corrosion or damage
Check refractory lining — freeze-thaw cycles can crack even well-cured refractory
Replace CO detector if more than 5 years old — electrochemical sensors degrade
Install fresh filter media — don't reuse media stored over winter
Check all gas line connections and replace any cracked hoses or fittings
Verify the pressure relief valve moves freely and hasn't corroded shut
Do a cold leak test before lighting — pressurize with air and check all joints
Run a short test fire (15–20 min) before connecting any load

consumables.heading: Consumables and what they cost
consumables.intro: A home gasifier has a short list of parts that wear out or need periodic replacement. Budget roughly $100–$200 per year for a system running 200–400 hours annually.

items.item: Filter media (wood chips, gravel, or commercial media)

log_tip.heading: Keep a maintenance log
log_tip.body: A simple notebook or spreadsheet tracking run hours, fuel used, filter changes, and any observations is worth more than any single maintenance task. Patterns in your log — increasing tar, rising pressure drop, more frequent ash removal — tell you what's changing before it becomes a problem. Date every entry.

cta.heading: Ready to build the system you'll maintain?
cta.body: Understanding maintenance before you build helps you design for serviceability — access panels, easy filter changes, and cleanout ports in the right places.
